newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FOCUS-Sri Lanka to boost low grown tea output.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sri Lanka to boost low grown tea output.

text.p: Small Sri Lankan tea growers, who helped generate a record crop last year, are getting state aid to improve output, set up new factories and overcome labour shortages, a government official said on Thursday.
"There are thousands of smallholders. They produce the bulk of the crop," Rohana Illangaratne, the chairman of the Tea Smallholdings Development Authority, told Reuters in an interview.
"They are not socially powerful to face challenges," he added. "So our aim is to form them into their own groups to make them stronger."
Illangaratne said the government will set up commercial nurseries to expand tea cultivation, provide seedlings for replanting and modernise tea factories to make good tea.
The government also plans to help small cultivators pack leaf in their villages and export directly to overseas markets, as well as set up new tea factories, he said.
The Indian Ocean island's 239,000 tea smallholders produce the bulk of the low grown teas, which now make up half the crop.
Most of the small cultivators own just one or two acres.
It was the rise in low grown tea output that helped increase total production by five percent to a record 258.4 million kg in 1996, Illangaratne said.
Low grown tea production rose by 16.3 million kg to 138.1 million kg from 121.8 million kg while the high grown and medium grown tea output actually fell.
Sri Lankan teas are categorised according to factory elevation -- high, medium and low.
The low growns, produced under 2,000 feet (600 metres) are much in demand in the Middle East and Russia, the world's biggest tea market.

Under a new aid programme launched with the help of loans from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), small cultivators will be organised into societies to replace middlemen in collection of green leaf and supply to factories to minimise exploitation, he said.
"We have to convert farmers into scientific farmers. Tea smallholders should not be tea smallholders for ever," he said. "We have achieved visible results in production and yields."

The average yield in smallholdings per hectare per year in made tea was 1,950 kg, some 1,020 kg higher than those on estates run by the newly-privatised plantation management firms where the average yield was a mere 930 kg, he said.
Small cultivators also used 89,000 tonnes of fertiliser last year, compared to 27,000 tonnes used by the plantation management companies, he added.
The authority has started training 3,300 youths in tea plucking and pruning to tackle the labour shortage in the low grown tea areas, mainly in the south, he said.
"The labour shortage is mainly due to lack of dignity of labour," he said. "We want to get across the message that working with soil is something you should be proud of."
Home gardening will be introduced into the school curriculum while small tea plots will be set up in schools in tea growning areas to teach students about tea cultivation and production, he said.
